items.stem: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency …
options: equal to that of visible light
items.answer: above about 20 kHz
items.markingKey: Above the upper limit of human hearing.

items.stem: Explain how an ultrasound transducer both produces and detects ultrasound.
items.answer: An alternating p.d. at the crystal's resonant frequency makes the piezoelectric crystal vibrate, producing ultrasound; returning echoes make the crystal vibrate, producing a small alternating p.d. that is detected.
items.markingKey: alternating p.d. → vibration (production) [1]; echo → vibration → p.d. (detection) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a coupling gel is necessary in an ultrasound scan.
items.answer: Air and skin have very different acoustic impedances, so almost all ultrasound would be reflected at the air–skin boundary; the gel has an impedance similar to skin and removes the air, so most ultrasound enters the body.
items.markingKey: large impedance difference air–skin [1]; gel matches impedance, transmission increased [1] [2]

items.stem: The density of soft tissue is 1060 kg m⁻³ and the speed of ultrasound in it is 1540 m s⁻¹. For bone the values are 1900 kg m⁻³ and 4080 m s⁻¹. Determine the specific acoustic impedance of soft tissue.
items.answer: 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹
items.markingKey: Z = ρc = 1060 × 1540 = 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The density of coupling gel is 1000 kg m⁻³ and the speed of ultrasound in it is 1500 m s⁻¹. For soft tissue the values are 1060 kg m⁻³ and 1540 m s⁻¹. Calculate the acoustic impedance of each and the intensity reflection coefficient at a coupling gel–soft tissue boundary.
items.markingKey: Z = ρc for both [1]; α = (Z₂ − Z₁)²/(Z₂ + Z₁)² [1]; = 0.00179 [1] [3]

items.stem: A sonographer in Nairobi uses ultrasound to image a bone–blood boundary. Data: density of bone 1900 kg m⁻³, speed 4080 m s⁻¹; density of blood 1060 kg m⁻³, speed 1570 m s⁻¹; air 430 kg m⁻² s⁻¹; gel 1.50 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. (a) Describe how ultrasound is produced by the transducer. (b) Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at the bone–blood boundary.
items.answer: (a) An alternating p.d. causes a piezoelectric crystal to vibrate (at resonance), emitting ultrasound. (b) 0.418
items.markingKey: (a) alternating p.d. on piezo crystal [1]; vibration produces ultrasound [1] [2] (b) α formula (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.418 [1] [2]

items.stem: How is ultrasound produced in a medical transducer?
options: a magnet is moved through a coil
an alternating p.d. makes a piezoelectric crystal vibrate
items.answer: an alternating p.d. makes a piezoelectric crystal vibrate
items.markingKey: Piezo crystal changes shape with applied p.d.; resonance at its natural frequency.

items.stem: Explain why ultrasound is reflected strongly at a boundary between soft tissue and bone.
items.answer: Bone has a much larger acoustic impedance than soft tissue; the reflection coefficient (Z₂ − Z₁)²/(Z₂ + Z₁)² is therefore large.
items.markingKey: large difference in Z [1]; large α [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a high frequency of ultrasound gives better resolution but less penetration.
items.answer: Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, so smaller details can be resolved; but attenuation increases with frequency, so it penetrates less deeply.
items.markingKey: shorter wavelength → finer detail [1]; more attenuation [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a high frequency of ultrasound gives better resolution but less penetration. (b) Explain why ultrasound is reflected strongly at a boundary between soft tissue and bone.

(b) Bone has a much larger acoustic impedance than soft tissue; the reflection coefficient (Z₂ − Z₁)²/(Z₂ + Z₁)² is therefore large.
items.markingKey: (a) shorter wavelength → finer detail [1]; more attenuation [1] [2] (b) large difference in Z [1]; large α [1] [2]

items.stem: An ultrasound pulse travels through soft tissue at 1590 m s⁻¹ and an echo from a boundary is received 65 μs after the pulse is emitted. Calculate the depth of the boundary below the transducer.
items.markingKey: d = ct/2 = 1590 × 6.50 × 10⁻⁵/2 = 5.17 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The density of fat is 925 kg m⁻³ and the speed of ultrasound in it is 1450 m s⁻¹. For water the values are 1000 kg m⁻³ and 1500 m s⁻¹. Determine the specific acoustic impedance of fat.
items.answer: 1.34 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹
items.markingKey: Z = ρc = 925 × 1450 = 1.34 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An ultrasound pulse travels through the liver at 1590 m s⁻¹ and an echo from a boundary is received 40 μs after the pulse is emitted. Calculate the depth of the boundary below the transducer.
items.markingKey: d = ct/2 = 1590 × 4.00 × 10⁻⁵/2 = 3.18 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An ultrasound pulse travels through the abdomen at 1540 m s⁻¹ and an echo from a boundary is received 78 μs after the pulse is emitted. Work out the depth of the boundary below the transducer.
items.markingKey: d = ct/2 = 1540 × 7.80 × 10⁻⁵/2 = 6.01 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: The density of coupling gel is 1000 kg m⁻³ and the speed of ultrasound in it is 1500 m s⁻¹. For blood the values are 1060 kg m⁻³ and 1570 m s⁻¹. Calculate the acoustic impedance of each and the intensity reflection coefficient at a coupling gel–blood boundary.
items.markingKey: Z = ρc for both [1]; α = (Z₂ − Z₁)²/(Z₂ + Z₁)² [1]; = 0.00269 [1] [3]

items.stem: The density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³ and the speed of ultrasound in it is 1500 m s⁻¹. For blood the values are 1060 kg m⁻³ and 1570 m s⁻¹. Ultrasound of intensity 10 mW cm⁻² is incident normally on a water–blood boundary. (a) Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient. (b) Calculate the reflected and transmitted intensities. (c) Explain whether this boundary would show up clearly on a scan.
items.answer: (a) 0.00269 (b) reflected 0.0269 mW cm⁻²; transmitted 9.97 mW cm⁻² (c) only faintly: the impedances are similar so little is reflected
items.markingKey: (a) Z values [1]; α = 0.00269 [1] (b) I_R = αI₀ [1]; I_T = (1 − α)I₀ [1] (c) judgement linked to α [1] [5]

items.stem: A sonographer in Hanoi uses ultrasound to image a fat–soft tissue boundary. Data: density of fat 925 kg m⁻³, speed 1450 m s⁻¹; density of soft tissue 1060 kg m⁻³, speed 1540 m s⁻¹; air 430 kg m⁻² s⁻¹; gel 1.50 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at an air–skin boundary, taking skin to have Z = 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹, and use it to explain why gel is used. (b) An echo from the boundary returns 65 μs after the pulse is sent through fat. Calculate the depth of the boundary.
items.answer: (a) 0.9989: almost all ultrasound would be reflected without gel (b) 4.71 cm
items.markingKey: (a) α ≈ 1 [1]; gel removes air / matches impedance [1] [2] (b) d = ct/2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.71 cm with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A sonographer in Hanoi uses ultrasound to image a blood–soft tissue boundary. Data: density of blood 1060 kg m⁻³, speed 1570 m s⁻¹; density of soft tissue 1060 kg m⁻³, speed 1540 m s⁻¹; air 430 kg m⁻² s⁻¹; gel 1.50 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the specific acoustic impedances of blood and soft tissue. (b) Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at an air–skin boundary, taking skin to have Z = 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹, and use it to explain why gel is used. (c) An echo from the boundary returns 40 μs after the pulse is sent through blood. Calculate the depth of the boundary.
items.answer: (a) 1.66 × 10⁶ and 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹ (b) 0.9989: almost all ultrasound would be reflected without gel (c) 3.14 cm
items.markingKey: (a) Z = ρc (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.66 × 10⁶ and 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) α ≈ 1 [1]; gel removes air / matches impedance [1] [2] (c) d = ct/2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.14 cm with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A medical student, Daniel, uses ultrasound to image a soft tissue–blood boundary. Data: density of soft tissue 1060 kg m⁻³, speed 1540 m s⁻¹; density of blood 1060 kg m⁻³, speed 1570 m s⁻¹; air 430 kg m⁻² s⁻¹; gel 1.50 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. (a) Describe how ultrasound is produced by the transducer. (b) Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at the soft tissue–blood boundary. (c) An echo from the boundary returns 90.0 μs after the pulse is sent through soft tissue. Calculate the depth of the boundary.
items.answer: (a) An alternating p.d. causes a piezoelectric crystal to vibrate (at resonance), emitting ultrasound. (b) 9.31 × 10⁻⁵ (c) 6.93 cm

items.stem: How are X-rays produced in an X-ray tube?
options: electrons are accelerated in a magnetic field
high-speed electrons are decelerated when they strike a metal target
a heated filament emits X-rays directly
radioactive nuclei in the target decay
items.answer: high-speed electrons are decelerated when they strike a metal target
items.markingKey: Bremsstrahlung plus characteristic lines.

items.stem: Explain why bones show up clearly on an X-ray image but soft tissues do not.
items.answer: Bone has a much larger attenuation coefficient than soft tissue, so far fewer X-rays pass through it; the large difference in transmitted intensity gives good contrast. Soft tissues have similar coefficients, so contrast is poor.
items.markingKey: bone μ much larger [1]; large difference in transmitted intensity → contrast [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the contrast of an X-ray image of soft tissue can be improved.
items.answer: Use a contrast medium with a high attenuation coefficient (e.g. barium or iodine) in the organ, or use lower-energy (softer) X-rays where absorption differences are greater.
items.markingKey: contrast medium (barium/iodine) [1]; reason: high μ / greater difference [1] [2]

items.stem: An X-ray tube operates with an accelerating p.d. of 40 kV and a tube current of 1.0 mA. Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays.
items.markingKey: λmin = hc/(eV) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁴) = 3.11 × 10⁻¹¹ m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An X-ray tube operates with an accelerating p.d. of 60 kV and a tube current of 100 mA. Calculate the maximum energy of an X-ray photon and the minimum wavelength.

A hospital X-ray tube in Auckland uses electrons accelerated through 80 kV onto a tungsten target. (a) Calculate the maximum energy of the X-ray photons in J. (b) Explain why the target must be cooled. (c) Explain why an aluminium filter is placed in the beam.
items.answer: (a) 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁴ J (b) About 99% of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes thermal energy in the target. (c) It absorbs low-energy (soft) X-rays that would be absorbed by the patient without reaching the detector, reducing dose.
items.markingKey: (a) E = eV: 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁴ J [1] (b) About 99% of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes thermal energy in the target [1] (c) absorbs soft X-rays [1]; reduces dose [1] [2]

items.stem: The minimum wavelength of X-rays from a tube operating at p.d. V is given by …
items.answer: hc/(eV)
items.markingKey: All the electron's KE eV goes into one photon.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The attenuation of a parallel X-ray beam in a material is described by … (b) How are X-rays produced in an X-ray tube?
items.answer: (a) I = I₀e^(−μx) (b) high-speed electrons are decelerated when they strike a metal target
items.markingKey: (a) Exponential attenuation with linear attenuation coefficient μ. (b) Bremsstrahlung plus characteristic lines.

items.stem: Describe the principles of CT scanning.
items.answer: An X-ray tube and detectors rotate around the patient; images of a thin slice are taken from many angles. A computer reconstructs the attenuation in each voxel of the slice, and slices are combined into a 3D image.
items.markingKey: many images from different angles of a slice [1]; computer reconstruction into 3D image of voxels [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why an X-ray tube has a continuous spectrum with a sharp minimum wavelength.
items.answer: Electrons decelerate in the target losing varying amounts of energy, producing photons of a continuous range of energies; the maximum photon energy equals the electron KE eV, giving λmin = hc/(eV).
items.markingKey: varying deceleration → continuous range [1]; maximum photon energy eV gives λmin [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of a CT scan compared with a single X-ray image.
items.answer: Advantages: 3D image, distinguishes overlapping structures and soft tissues with small attenuation differences. Disadvantage: much larger radiation dose (and cost, time).
items.markingKey: advantage [1]; disadvantage (dose) [1] [2]

items.stem: An X-ray tube operates with an accelerating p.d. of 40 kV and a tube current of 20 mA. What is the minimum wavelength of the X-rays?
A parallel beam of X-rays passes through 3.0 cm of bone, whose linear attenuation coefficient for these X-rays is 3.0 cm⁻¹. Calculate the fraction of the intensity transmitted.
items.markingKey: I/I₀ = e^(−μx) = e^(−3.0 × 3.0) = 1.23 × 10⁻⁴. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An X-ray tube operates with an accelerating p.d. of 100 kV and a tube current of 1.0 mA. Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays.

items.stem: A PET scan uses a tracer that emits …
items.answer: positrons (β⁺ particles)
items.markingKey: Positron emission tomography.

items.stem: When a positron meets an electron they annihilate, producing …
options: two γ-ray photons moving in opposite directions
items.answer: two γ-ray photons moving in opposite directions
items.markingKey: Momentum conservation requires two photons in opposite directions.

items.stem: Explain why a PET tracer must have a short half-life and why it is produced near the hospital.
items.answer: A short half-life (minutes to hours) gives high activity for the scan and reduces the dose afterwards; because it decays quickly, it must be made (in a cyclotron) close to where it is used.
items.markingKey: short t½ reduces dose / high activity [1]; decays quickly so made nearby [1] [2]

items.stem: An electron and a positron, both effectively at rest, annihilate in a patient's tissue during a PET scan. Calculate the energy of each γ-ray photon produced.
items.markingKey: E = mₑc² = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cancer clinic in Jakarta injects a patient with a tracer labelled with nitrogen-13, which decays by β⁺ emission with a half-life of 9.97 minutes. (a) Calculate the energy of each annihilation photon in MeV. (b) Calculate the fraction of the tracer remaining after 39.9 minutes.
items.markingKey: (a) E = mₑc² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.512 MeV with unit [1] [2] (b) 4 half-lives: 0.0625 [1]

items.stem: What is the energy of each photon produced when an electron and a positron at rest annihilate?
items.markingKey: Each photon carries mₑc².

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) When a positron meets an electron they annihilate, producing … (b) In a PET scanner, the location of the annihilation is found from …
items.answer: (a) two γ-ray photons moving in opposite directions (b) the difference in arrival times of the two photons at detectors on opposite sides
items.markingKey: (a) Momentum conservation requires two photons in opposite directions. (b) Coincidence detection along a line of response.

items.stem: Explain how a PET scan produces an image of metabolic activity.
items.answer: The tracer (e.g. FDG) is taken up most by active cells; positrons from it annihilate with electrons, producing pairs of γ-photons detected simultaneously by a ring of detectors. Lines of response and timing differences locate the sources, and a computer builds up an image of tracer concentration.
items.markingKey: tracer concentrates in active tissue [1]; coincident photon pairs located → image [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the two annihilation photons each have energy mₑc² when the electron and positron are almost at rest.
items.answer: The total energy available is the rest energy 2mₑc² (kinetic energy negligible); two photons with equal and opposite momenta must have equal energies, so each has mₑc².
items.markingKey: total energy 2mₑc² [1]; shared equally (momentum) [1] [2]

items.stem: In a PET scan, each annihilation photon has energy 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. What is the frequency of each photon?
A dose of FDG containing fluorine-18 (half-life 110 minutes) has an activity of 300 MBq when prepared. The scan begins 45 minutes later. Calculate the activity at the start of the scan.
items.answer: 226 MBq

items.stem: A dose of FDG containing fluorine-18 (half-life 110 minutes) has an activity of 300 MBq when prepared. The scan begins 30 minutes later. Calculate the activity at the start of the scan.
items.answer: 248 MBq

items.stem: In a PET scan, a positron annihilates with an electron, both effectively at rest. Calculate the energy of each photon produced, in J and in MeV, and its wavelength.

A cancer clinic in Bangkok injects a patient with a tracer labelled with carbon-11, which decays by β⁺ emission with a half-life of 20.4 minutes. (a) Describe what happens to the positron emitted. (b) The two photons from one annihilation arrive at opposite detectors 0.30 ns apart. Calculate the distance of the annihilation from the midpoint between the detectors.
items.answer: (a) It travels a very short distance in tissue and annihilates with an electron, producing two γ-photons in opposite directions. (b) 4.5 cm
items.markingKey: (a) annihilates with electron [1]; two photons opposite [1] [2] (b) cΔt/2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.5 cm with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A PET centre in Cairo injects a patient with a tracer labelled with nitrogen-13, which decays by β⁺ emission with a half-life of 9.97 minutes. (a) Calculate the fraction of the tracer remaining after 19.9 minutes. (b) The two photons from one annihilation arrive at opposite detectors 0.30 ns apart. Calculate the distance of the annihilation from the midpoint between the detectors. (c) Explain why the tracer must be produced close to the hospital.
items.answer: (a) 0.25 (b) 4.5 cm (c) Its short half-life means it would decay significantly during transport.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the advantages and disadvantages of a CT scan compared with a single X-ray image. (b) Explain why an X-ray tube has a continuous spectrum with a sharp minimum wavelength.
items.answer: (a) Advantages: 3D image, distinguishes overlapping structures and soft tissues with small attenuation differences. Disadvantage: much larger radiation dose (and cost, time). (b) Electrons decelerate in the target losing varying amounts of energy, producing photons of a continuous range of energies; the maximum photon energy equals the electron KE eV, giving λmin = hc/(eV).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why bones show up clearly on an X-ray image but soft tissues do not. (b) Explain why an X-ray tube has a continuous spectrum with a sharp minimum wavelength.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a high frequency of ultrasound gives better resolution but less penetration. (b) Explain how an ultrasound transducer both produces and detects ultrasound.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a coupling gel is necessary in an ultrasound scan. (b) Explain how an ultrasound transducer both produces and detects ultrasound.
items.answer: (a) Air and skin have very different acoustic impedances, so almost all ultrasound would be reflected at the air–skin boundary; the gel has an impedance similar to skin and removes the air, so most ultrasound enters the body. (b) An alternating p.d. at the crystal's resonant frequency makes the piezoelectric crystal vibrate, producing ultrasound; returning echoes make the crystal vibrate, producing a small alternating p.d. that is detected.

items.answer: (a) An X-ray tube and detectors rotate around the patient; images of a thin slice are taken from many angles. Soft tissues have similar coefficients, so contrast is poor.
